name: Red Lake agreement under the Nelson Act, signed July 8, 1889 (diminished Red Lake Reservation kept by the Red Lake and Pembina bands)
aka: Nelson Act agreement with the Red Lake Chippewa
citation: Act of January 14, 1889, ch. 24, 25 Stat. 642; agreement printed in H. R. Ex. Doc. 247, 51st Cong., 1st sess.
nations: Red Lake Band of Chippewa Indians (Miskwaagamiiwi-Zaaga'iganiwi Anishinaabeg)
the other Chippewa (Ojibwe) of Minnesota, whose assent the Act required for the Red Lake cession
promises: The Red Lake bands kept a diminished reservation around Lower Red Lake and the western part of Upper Red Lake, bounded as the agreement described from the Thief River to the upper and lower lakes, Hay Creek and the Clearwater River (Royce, area 707).

Section 1: the Red Lake cession was valid only if assented to in writing by two-thirds of the male adults of all the Chippewa in Minnesota and approved by the President; Indians already holding allotments were not to be disturbed without their own consent.
Section 3: the Red Lake Indians were to be allotted land in severalty on the Red Lake Reservation, not removed to White Earth.

Sections 4 to 6: ceded pine lands to be examined, appraised at no less than $3 per thousand feet of pine and sold at public auction in 40-acre parcels for no less than the appraised value; other ceded land sold only to actual settlers under the homestead law at $1.25 an acre.

Section 7: net proceeds held in the Treasury as a permanent fund for all the Chippewa in Minnesota at 5 percent interest for fifty years, half the interest paid to heads of families, a quarter per capita and a quarter for schools, with the fund then divided in equal shares; the United States to advance $90,000 a year as interest until the fund reached $3,000,000.

breaches.what: Red Lake Nation leaders say the United States used fraud and deception in negotiating the 1889 agreement, and that the government's map after the talks split Upper Red Lake rather than following the outline the chiefs had drawn, which the chiefs called false at the time.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Red Lake Tribal Chairman Darrell Seki Sr. and Tribal Secretary Sam Strong, as reported by the Bemidji Pioneer

source.title: Red Lake Nation takes steps to restore east boundary of Upper Red Lake (Bemidji Pioneer, March 25, 2023, by Daltyn Lofstrom)

breaches.quote: fraud and deception on the part of the United States in negotiating the 1889 agreement with the Red Lake chiefs

today: Royce shows area 707 as the diminished Red Lake Reservation. Red Lake Nation leaders said in 2023 they were asking the United States to restore the east boundary of Upper Red Lake and would likely sue if refused. The separate claim that the 1889 cession was taken without consent failed in 1972 on the Court of Claims' 1935 finding that the required assent was given.

nationVoice.summary: Tribal Chairman Darrell Seki Sr. says the United States used fraud and deception in negotiating the 1889 agreement, that the government map produced afterwards split Upper Red Lake instead of following the outline the chiefs drew, and that the chiefs rejected that map at the time; Tribal Secretary Sam Strong calls the loss of the lake a theft.

openQuestions: The agreement itself (H. R. Ex. Doc. 247, 51st Cong., 1st sess.) was not opened; its terms here are the Nelson Act's, which the agreement accepted, and Royce's description.

Docket 189 (Red Lake Band, 1973) concerns pre-1889 survey errors that excluded Tracts A and C from the reservation; it is not a finding on this agreement and is left out. The outcome of the Red Lake accounting claims (Dockets 189-A and 189-B) after their 1976 transfer to the Court of Claims was not found.
The Red Lake Nation's own website was not opened; its account here comes from leaders quoted in a newspaper.

treaties.json lists Rocky Boy's, Turtle Mountain and White Earth as present-day tribes for this entry but not the Red Lake Band by its own name first; Royce names the Red Lake Chippewa as the band that signed on July 8, 1889, with the Pembina signing on July 29, 1889.

Royce's area 707 is land the bands kept, not land they gave up; the breach claimed here is the boundary of what was kept (Upper Red Lake), which rests on the Nation's statement only. The 1902 and 1904 Red Lake cessions belong to their own entries.

Audit 2026-11-08: treaties.json duplicate. This entry and cession-1889-07-08-chippewa-of-minnesota are the same Red Lake agreement signed July 8, 1889 (Royce, Signed July 8, 1889); Royce area 707 is the diminished reservation kept, not a cession, so treaties.json labelling it a cession of the Red Lake and Pembina bands is an error. The map should not count the agreement twice.

plain.promised: In the 1889 agreement the Red Lake bands kept a smaller reservation around Lower Red Lake and part of Upper Red Lake, with the rest sold for a fund for all the Chippewa in Minnesota.
plain.happened: No court or claims commission finding of a breach was found. Red Lake Nation leaders say the government's map after the talks split Upper Red Lake, unlike the outline the chiefs drew, and that the agreement was obtained by fraud and deception.
plain.today: In 2023 the Nation was asking the United States to restore the east boundary of Upper Red Lake and said it would likely sue if refused.
